definition: In mathematical optimization, Zadeh's rule (also known as the least-entered rule) is an algorithmic refinement of the simplex method for linear optimization.
details: The rule was proposed around 1980 by Norman Zadeh (son of Lotfi A. Zadeh), and has entered the folklore of convex optimization since then. Zadeh offered a reward of $1,000 to anyone who can show that the rule admits polynomially many iterations or to prove that there is a family of linear programs on which the pivoting rule requires subexponentially many iterations to find the optimum.

explainer.lead: Zadeh's rule, also called the least-entered rule, is an algorithmic refinement of the simplex method for linear optimization. It matters because it is a long-standing open question in convex optimization whether this pivoting rule is efficient.

tiers.eli5: It's a tie-breaking rule for choosing the next step in a classic optimization algorithm, and nobody knows if it always finishes quickly.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers meet it as a pivoting rule inside simplex-based linear solvers. A pitfall is assuming its performance is polynomial; whether it is remains unproven.
tiers.paperLevel: It is a least-entered pivoting rule for the simplex method, proposed around 1980 by Norman Zadeh; it is unknown whether it admits polynomially many iterations, or whether some family of linear programs requires subexponentially many.
